en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section First Chapter
The Discussion on Abandoning: The Discussion on Not Quoting from the Suttas.
Does the worldling abandon sensual lust and ill will?

“Yes. [The interlocutor asks: “Does one abandon it absolutely? Does one abandon it without remainder? Does one abandon it so that there is no rebirth-linking? Does one abandon it together with its root? Does one abandon it together with craving?
Does one abandon it together with the underlying tendencies? Does one abandon it by means of noble knowledge? Does one abandon it by means of the noble path? Is it unshakable?”
Is it that one abandons [the defilements] while penetrating [the path], or does one abandon them while realizing the fruit of non-returning?
One should not say so … [as before] … Does an ordinary person suppress sensual lust and ill will?
Yes. It suppresses absolutely; it suppresses without remainder; it suppresses so as to prevent rebirth; it suppresses with its roots;
it suppresses together with craving; it suppresses together with underlying tendencies; it suppresses by means of noble knowledge.
Does one suppress sensual desire and ill will by means of the noble path, suppress them while penetrating the unshakable, and suppress them while realizing the fruit of non-returning?
One should not say so …pe….
Does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual desire and ill will, and does he abandon them absolutely and without remainder? …pe….
Is it true that one who realizes the fruit of non-returning abandons [these]? Yes.
Does an ordinary person abandon sensual lust and ill will, and does he abandon them absolutely, abandoning them without remainder? …pe…
Is it the case that one who realizes the fruit of non-returning abandons [the defilements]?
One should not say so …pe….
A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning suppresses sensual desire and ill will; and he suppresses them absolutely, suppresses them without remainder …pe….
Is it the case that one who realizes the fruit of non-returning suppresses [the defilements]? Yes.
An ordinary person suppresses sensual lust and ill will, and he suppresses them absolutely, suppresses them without remainder …pe…
Is it not the case that one who realizes the fruit of non-returning suppresses [the defilements]?
One should certainly not say so …pe….
An ordinary person abandons sensual lust and ill-will, yet he does not abandon them absolutely, nor does he abandon them without remainder …pe….
Is it not the case that one who is realizing the fruit of non-returning abandons [these]?
Yes, it is.
Does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual lust and ill will, yet not abandon them absolutely? ...pe... Yes, he does.
Is it not the case that one who realizes the fruit of non-returning does not abandon [the defilements]?
One should certainly not say so …pe….
An ordinary person suppresses sensual desire and ill will, yet he does not suppress them absolutely, nor does he suppress them without remainder …pe….
Is it not the case that one who is realizing the fruit of non-returning suppresses [the defilements]?
Yes, it is.
A person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning suppresses sensual lust and ill will; yet he does not suppress them absolutely, nor does he suppress them without remainder …pe…
Is it not the case that one who realizes the fruit of non-returning does not suppress [the defilements]?
One should certainly not say so …pe… Does an ordinary person abandon sensual lust and ill will?
“Yes,” he replied. “By what path?
“By the path belonging to the realm of form.”

Is the path of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) leading out, leading to destruction, leading to enlightenment, leading to diminution, free from taints (anāsava), not conducive to fetters (asaṃyojaniya), not conducive to knots (aganthaniya), not conducive to floods (anoghaniya), not conducive to yokes (ayoganiya), not conducive to hindrances (anīvaraṇiya), unclung-to (aparāmaṭṭha), not subject to clinging (anupādāniya), and not subject to defilement (asaṅkilesiya)?
One should not say so.

Is it not the case that the path of the fine-material sphere is not leading out, does not lead to destruction, does not lead to enlightenment, does not lead to diminution, is with taints, conducive to fetters, and so forth, up to: conducive to defilement?
“Yes.

[The opponent asks: “If the path belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) is not leading out, does not go to destruction, and so forth, and is subject to defilement, then indeed you should not say:”
“The worldling abandons sensual lust and ill will by means of the fine-material-sphere path.

Does a person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual lust and ill will by means of the non-returning path; and is that path leading out, leading to destruction, leading to enlightenment, leading to diminution, untainted … [and] non-afflicted?
“Yes.

“Does an ordinary person abandon sensual lust and ill will by means of a path belonging to the fine-material sphere? And is that path leading out, leading to destruction, leading to enlightenment, leading to diminution, untainted … [and so on] … non-defiled?”

It should not be said thus … [as before] … Does the worldling abandon sensual lust and ill will by means of a fine-material-sphere path? And is that path non-leading-out, not leading to destruction, not leading to enlightenment, not leading to diminution, with taints … [as before] … subject to defilement?
“Yes.

[The opponent asks: “Does the person practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual lust and ill will by means of the path of non-returning, and yet that path is not leading out, does not lead to destruction, does not lead to enlightenment, does not lead to diminution, and is with taints … down to … subject to defilement?”

It should not be said so … [as before] … Is it the case that an ordinary person who is free from lust for sensual pleasures, through the simultaneous realization of the Dhamma, is established in the fruit of non-returning?
Yes.
"Does one establish oneself in arahantship?
"One should not say so... [and so on] ...
"Does an ordinary person who is free from passion for sense-pleasures establish themselves in the fruit of non-returning simultaneously with the realization of the Dhamma?"
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then one develops the three paths simultaneously, neither before nor after?
One should not speak thus… [and so on].
Is it the case that one develops the three paths neither before nor after [one another]?
Yes. Does one realize the three fruits of recluseship neither before nor after [one another]? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … “Does one realize the three fruits of recluseship neither before nor after?
Yes.
Is there a convergence of three types of contact, three types of feeling, three types of perception,
three types of volition, three types of consciousness, three types of faith, three types of energy, three types of mindfulness,
three types of concentration, and three types of wisdom?

It should not be said so … [as before] … Is it the case that an ordinary person who is free from lust for sensual pleasures, through the simultaneous realization of the Dhamma, becomes established in the fruit of non-returning?
Yes.
"Is it by the path of stream-entry?
One should not say so... [and so on] ... "Is it by the path of once-returning? One should not say so.
It should not be stated thus.
By which path? By the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga).
"Does one abandon personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances by means of the path of non-returning?
"One should not say so... [and so on].
The Discussion on Citing Suttas.
Is it not the case that one abandons the view of a self-identity, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances by means of the path of non-returning?
Yes, it is.
But has it not been stated by the Blessed One that the fruit of stream-entry is attained through the abandoning of these three fetters?
“Yes.
“If the Blessed One has stated that the fruit of stream-entry results from the abandoning of the three fetters, then surely it cannot be said:
‘By the path of the non-returner, one abandons personality-belief, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances.’”
Is it not to be said that one abandons gross sensual desire and gross ill will by means of the path of non-returning?
… [as before] … Is it not to be said that one abandons gross sensual desire and gross ill will by means of the path of non-returning?
“Yes.
“But is it not stated by the Blessed One that the fruit of the once-returner is attained through the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will?
“Yes.”
If the fruit of the once-returner was spoken of by the Blessed One because of the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will, then surely it should not be said:
“By the path of the non-returner, one abandons gross sensual lust and gross ill will.
Does an ordinary person who has become free from lust for sense pleasures, through the simultaneous realization of the Dhamma, abide in the fruit of the non-returner?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are all those who realize the Dhamma established in the fruit of non-returning simultaneously with that realization of the Dhamma?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] … .
Is it not to be said that "the worldling abandons sensual lust and ill will"?
Yes, it is.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“In the past,
there were those six renowned teachers;”
Free from the stench of raw flesh, devoted to compassion,
they have transcended the fetter of sensual desire.
Having faded away from lust for sense-pleasures,
They went to the Brahma-world;
there were many hundreds of their disciples as well.
Free from the stench of raw flesh, devoted to compassion,
having transcended the fetter of sensual desire,
and having faded away from lust for sense-pleasures—
“They have gone to the Brahma-world.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
"Therefore, the worldling abandons sensual lust and ill will.
Does the worldling abandon sensual lust and ill will?
Yes, he does.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:

“Indeed, monks, that teacher Sunetta, though he was so long-lived and remained for so long, was not yet liberated from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he was not yet liberated from suffering, I say.”
For what reason?
Because of the non-awakening and non-penetration of four things. Which four?
It is through the non-awakening and non-penetration of noble virtue, the non-awakening and non-penetration of noble concentration, noble wisdom, and noble liberation.
But now, monks, this noble virtue has been awakened to and penetrated; noble concentration has been awakened to and penetrated;
noble wisdom has been awakened to and penetrated; noble liberation has been awakened to and penetrated.
“Craving for existence has been cut off, the conduit to existence is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.
“Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation;”
"These phenomena have been fully understood by the illustrious Gotama.
Thus, having realized this through direct knowledge, the Buddha—
He proclaimed the Dhamma to the bhikkhus;
the Teacher, the Seer who brings an end to suffering, has attained final Nibbāna.
Is this indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“The worldling abandons sensual lust and ill will.
The Discussion on Abandoning is finished.
